games.title: Review — Skin, Embryology, Spine & Skull: quick quiz
games.blurb: Quiz for Year 1 and above, written fresh today.

questions.q: Which mechanoreceptor located in the dermal papillae is primarily responsible for detecting fine touch and low-frequency vibration?
questions.explanation: Meissner corpuscles are rapidly adapting mechanoreceptors located within dermal papillae that sense light touch and low-frequency vibration.

questions.q: The nucleus pulposus of an intervertebral disc is an adult remnant of which embryonic structure?
questions.explanation: The nucleus pulposus derives from the embryonic notochord, whereas the outer annulus fibrosus develops from the sclerotome.

questions.q: Which spinal ligament directly acts to prevent hyperextension of the vertebral column?
questions.explanation: The anterior longitudinal ligament runs along the anterior surface of the vertebral bodies and is the only spinal ligament that limits hyperextension.

questions.q: The middle meningeal artery enters the cranial cavity by passing through which foramen?
questions.explanation: The middle meningeal artery enters the middle cranial fossa through the foramen spinosum.

questions.q: Which cranial suture separates the frontal bone from the two parietal bones?
questions.explanation: The coronal suture runs laterally across the skull to separate the anterior frontal bone from the posterior parietal bones.

questions.q: Meckel's cartilage and the mandibular prominence develop from which pharyngeal arch?
questions.explanation: The first pharyngeal arch (mandibular arch) gives rise to Meckel's cartilage, the mandible, malleus, and incus.

questions.q: Epidermal stem cells capable of continuous mitotic division are primarily located in which layer of the epidermis?
questions.explanation: The stratum basale is the innermost layer of the epidermis containing stem cells that undergo rapid mitosis to replenish keratinocytes.

questions.q: Which anatomical feature is unique to thoracic vertebrae when compared to cervical and lumbar vertebrae?
questions.explanation: Thoracic vertebrae possess costal facets on their bodies and transverse processes for articulation with the ribs.

questions.q: Which cranial bone contains the sella turcica, the bony depression that houses the pituitary gland?
questions.explanation: The sella turcica is a saddle-like prominence located on the superior surface of the body of the sphenoid bone.

questions.q: During vertebral column development, sclerotomes undergo a process where the caudal half of one sclerotome fuses with the cranial half of the subadjacent sclerotome. What is this process called?
questions.explanation: Resegmentation of sclerotomes allows spinal nerves to emerge between vertebrae and intervertebral muscles to cross intervertebral joints.

games.title: Aplastic Anemia: Causes, Symptoms & Treatment Haematology: quick quiz
games.topic: Aplastic Anemia: Causes, Symptoms & Treatment Haematology
games.blurb: Quiz for Year 3 and above, written fresh today.

questions.q: Which bone marrow biopsy finding is most characteristic of severe aplastic anemia?
options: Markedly hypocellular marrow replaced predominantly by fat cells
Extensive fibrosis with teardrop-shaped red cells
questions.explanation: Aplastic anemia is characterized by pancytopenia and a hypocellular bone marrow where normal hematopoietic elements are replaced by adipose tissue.

questions.q: A 24-year-old male presents with fatigue, easy bruising, and mucosal bleeding. Labs show pancytopenia. Which physical exam finding would most strongly argue AGAINST a primary diagnosis of aplastic anemia?
questions.explanation: Splenomegaly is typically absent in idiopathic aplastic anemia, and its presence suggests an alternative diagnosis such as leukemia, lymphoma, or portal hypertension.

questions.q: A 7-year-old child presents with pancytopenia, skin hyperpigmentation, thumb abnormalities, and short stature. Which inherited bone marrow failure syndrome is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Fanconi anemia is an autosomal recessive DNA repair defect characterized by progressive bone marrow failure, short stature, radial/thumb ray defects, and hyperpigmentation.

questions.q: Which medication is historically associated with dose-independent, idiosyncratic aplastic anemia?
questions.explanation: Chloramphenicol is well-known for causing a rare, idiosyncratic, and often fatal aplastic anemia that is independent of the administered dose.

questions.q: Infection with which agent is a recognized cause of severe aplastic anemia, typically developing 1 to 3 months after an episode of acute liver inflammation?
questions.explanation: Hepatitis-associated aplastic anemia typically occurs 1 to 3 months following an episode of acute seronegative (non-A-E) hepatitis.

questions.q: According to standard diagnostic criteria, which peripheral blood laboratory parameter supports the classification of aplastic anemia as severe?
questions.explanation: Severe aplastic anemia requires bone marrow cellularity <25% plus at least two criteria: absolute neutrophil count <0.5 × 10^9/L, platelet count <20 × 10^9/L, or absolute reticulocyte count <20 × 10^9/L.

questions.q: What is the primary pathophysiologic mechanism responsible for hematopoietic stem cell destruction in most cases of acquired aplastic anemia?
options: Autoreactive cytotoxic T-cell destruction of stem cells
Complement-mediated lysis via the alternative pathway
Immune complex deposition in the marrow stroma
questions.explanation: Acquired aplastic anemia is primarily mediated by autoreactive CD8+ cytotoxic T-lymphocytes producing type 1 cytokines that trigger apoptosis of hematopoietic progenitor cells.

questions.q: What is the first-line curative treatment of choice for a 19-year-old patient with severe aplastic anemia who has an HLA-matched sibling?
options: Combination immunosuppressive therapy with ATG and cyclosporine
questions.explanation: Allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation from an HLA-identical sibling is the preferred curative treatment for young patients with severe aplastic anemia.

questions.q: For an adult patient with severe aplastic anemia who lacks an HLA-matched sibling donor, which combination represents the standard first-line medical therapy?
questions.explanation: Standard immunosuppressive therapy for patients unsuitable for immediate transplantation consists of horse ATG, cyclosporine, and the thrombopoietin receptor agonist eltrombopag.

questions.q: A peripheral blood smear from a patient with uncomplicated idiopathic aplastic anemia typically displays which morphologic characteristic?
options: Normocytic normochromic red cells with marked reticulocytopenia
Prominent schistocytes and nucleated red blood cells
Extensive leukocytosis with immature blast cells
Teardrop cells (dacryocytes) and a leukoerythroblastic picture
questions.explanation: Aplastic anemia produces pancytopenia with morphologically normal normocytic, normochromic red cells and a characteristically low reticulocyte count without dysplastic or immature circulating cells.

games.title: Cardiomyopathies (EXTRA): case showdown
games.blurb: Case Showdown for Year 4 and above, written fresh today.

questions.q: A 68-year-old postmenopausal female presents with sudden-onset substernal chest pain immediately following the news of her spouse's sudden death. Coronary angiography demonstrates non-obstructed, normal coronary arteries, while echocardiography shows left ventricular apical ballooning with hyperkinesis of the basal segments. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Takotsubo (stress-induced) cardiomyopathy typically affects postmenopausal women following severe emotional or physical stress and manifests as transient apical ballooning in the absence of obstructive coronary disease.

questions.q: A 24-year-old male athlete collapses during a soccer match and is resuscitated from ventricular fibrillation. An ECG shows T-wave inversions in leads V1–V3 and an epsilon wave, while echocardiography reveals right ventricular dilation and localized aneurysm formation. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy (ARVC) features fibrofatty replacement of the right ventricular myocardium, predisposing patients to ventricular arrhythmias and characteristic ECG changes such as epsilon waves.

questions.q: A 72-year-old male presents with progressive exertional dyspnea, peripheral edema, and a history of bilateral carpal tunnel release surgery. An ECG displays strikingly low QRS voltage despite an echocardiogram demonstrating marked concentric ventricular hypertrophy with a bright, 'speckled' myocardial appearance. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Cardiac amyloidosis presents as a restrictive cardiomyopathy often associated with carpal tunnel syndrome, low QRS voltage on ECG, and a classic speckled pattern on echocardiography.

questions.q: A 31-year-old G2P2 female presents 3 weeks after an uncomplicated vaginal delivery with progressive orthopnea, nocturnal dyspnea, and bilateral ankle swelling. Echocardiography shows global left ventricular hypokinesis with an ejection fraction of 28%, and she has no prior cardiac history. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Peripartum cardiomyopathy is an idiopathic dilated cardiomyopathy marked by heart failure with reduced ejection fraction developing late in pregnancy or in the months immediately following delivery.

questions.q: A 45-year-old male originally from rural South America presents with signs of heart failure, dysphagia due to megaesophagus, and a right bundle branch block on ECG. Echocardiography demonstrates diffuse left ventricular dilation with a prominent apical aneurysm. What is the most likely underlying etiology?
questions.explanation: Chagas disease, caused by Trypanosoma cruzi, is a major cause of dilated cardiomyopathy in Latin America and is frequently associated with conduction blockages and gastrointestinal megaganglionosis (e.g., megaesophagus).

questions.q: A 52-year-old male with a 20-year history of heavy daily alcohol consumption presents with bilateral leg swelling, fatigue, and orthopnea. Echocardiography demonstrates biventricular enlargement with an ejection fraction of 25%, and coronary angiography shows clean arteries. What is the primary initial intervention to potentially reverse his myocardial dysfunction?
questions.explanation: Alcoholic cardiomyopathy is a toxin-induced dilated cardiomyopathy that can be partially or completely reversed with strict alcohol abstinence.

questions.q: A 50-year-old male presents with hyperpigmented skin, newly diagnosed diabetes mellitus, fatigue, and signs of heart failure. Cardiac MRI confirms significant iron deposition within the myocardium. What type of cardiomyopathy does iron overload typically produce early in its disease course?
questions.explanation: Cardiac hemochromatosis initially causes iron deposition leading to a restrictive cardiomyopathy, which may later progress to a dilated pattern as heart failure advances.

questions.q: A 38-year-old female with known pulmonary sarcoidosis presents to the emergency department after a syncopal episode. An ECG reveals complete (third-degree) atrioventricular block and non-sustained ventricular tachycardia. Which diagnostic modality is most appropriate to evaluate for active cardiac sarcoidosis involvement?
options: Endomyocardial biopsy of the right atrium
questions.explanation: Advanced cardiac imaging with cardiac MRI (late gadolinium enhancement) or FDG-PET is the non-invasive modality of choice for identifying active inflammation and scarring in cardiac sarcoidosis.

games.title: Hepatic Amoebiasis: case showdown
games.blurb: Case Showdown for Year 4 and above, written fresh today.

questions.q: A 42-year-old man presents with a 2-week history of right upper quadrant pain, high-grade fever, and weight loss. He recently returned from a trip to endemic rural Mexico. Examination reveals tenderness in the right hypochondrium and hepatomegaly, and abdominal ultrasound demonstrates a single, hypoechoic, round lesion in the right lobe of the liver. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Amebic liver abscess classically presents with fever, right upper quadrant pain, and a solitary hypoechoic lesion in the right lobe of the liver in a traveler from an endemic area.

questions.q: A 35-year-old male is evaluated for a 10-day history of intermittent fever and dull right upper quadrant abdominal pain. Laboratory studies show leukocytosis and an elevated alkaline phosphatase, but normal transaminases. Serology for Entamoeba histolytica is strongly positive, and ultrasound shows a 6 cm cavity containing debris in the right hepatic lobe. What is the most appropriate initial medical management?
questions.explanation: Metronidazole is the first-line tissue amoebicide used to treat invasive amebic infections, including amebic liver abscesses.

questions.q: A 50-year-old woman with a large amebic liver abscess in the right lobe of the liver is initiated on oral metronidazole with good symptomatic response. To completely eradicate the luminal colonization of Entamoeba histolytica and prevent relapse, what additional medication should be prescribed?
questions.explanation: A luminal agent such as paromomycin or iodoquinol must be given following tissue amoebicides to eradicate cysts in the colon and prevent recurrence.

questions.q: A 28-year-old male presents with severe right-sided pleuritic chest pain and dyspnea in addition to right upper quadrant abdominal pain. Imaging reveals an amebic liver abscess of the right hepatic lobe that has ruptured through the diaphragm into the pleural space. What is the most common direction of rupture for a right hepatic lobe amebic abscess?
questions.explanation: Abscesses in the superior portion of the right lobe of the liver most frequently rupture superiorly through the diaphragm into the pleural space or lung.

questions.q: A 45-year-old man undergoes ultrasound-guided needle aspiration of a suspected liver abscess yielding 'anchovy paste' or 'chocolate sauce' colored fluid. Gram stain and cultures of the aspirate are negative. Which organism is the classic cause of this finding?
questions.explanation: The necrotic debris and lysed tissue of an amebic liver abscess characteristically yields reddish-brown 'anchovy paste' fluid that is typically sterile on bacterial culture.

questions.q: A 39-year-old immigrant from Southeast Asia presents with fever and right upper quadrant pain. Ultrasound shows a liver mass, and indirect hemagglutination assay (IHA) for Entamoeba histolytica is negative. However, symptoms persist despite broad-spectrum antibiotics. What is the most likely reason for the negative serology early in the disease course?
options: Antibodies may not have had sufficient time to develop
Serology is only positive after surgical drainage
Entamoeba histolytica does not elicit an antibody response
Cross-reactivity with normal flora suppresses titers
questions.explanation: Serology for amebiasis can occasionally be false-negative in the first week of symptom onset before a measurable humoral immune response has developed.

questions.q: A 60-year-old male with a 10 cm amebic liver abscess near the dome of the liver shows no clinical improvement after 72 hours of appropriate intravenous metronidazole therapy. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.explanation: Therapeutic percutaneous aspiration or catheter drainage is indicated if there is a lack of clinical response to medical therapy within 3-5 days, risk of rupture, or a very large abscess.

questions.q: A 44-year-old male evaluated for a solitary liver abscess reports a history of dysentery with bloody stools several weeks prior to the onset of his right upper quadrant pain. Stool microscopy at that time showed trophozoites containing ingested erythrocytes. What is the causative pathogen?
questions.explanation: Entamoeba histolytica trophozoites classically ingest red blood cells (erythrophagocytosis), which helps differentiate them from non-pathogenic intestinal amoebae.

games.title: Gene Transfer: drug duel
games.blurb: Drug Duel for Year 2 and above, written fresh today.

questions.q: Which of the following viral vectors is most commonly derived from a parvovirus and requires a helper virus like an adenovirus for efficient replication in gene therapy applications?
questions.explanation: Adeno-associated virus (AAV) is a small, replication-deficient parvovirus widely used in gene therapy due to its low immunogenicity and requirement for a helper virus to replicate.

questions.q: What is the primary mechanism by which retroviral vectors mediate stable, long-term gene transfer in target cells?
options: Episomal persistence in the nucleus without replication
Random integration of the proviral cDNA into the host cell genome
Direct translation of injected viral mRNA in the cytoplasm
Homologous recombination exclusively at the native gene locus
questions.explanation: Retroviral vectors mediate stable gene transfer by reverse-transcribing their RNA into cDNA, which then randomly integrates into the host cell's chromosomal DNA.

questions.q: Which named gene therapy product is approved for the treatment of spinal muscular atrophy (SMA) type 1 and utilizes a self-complementary adeno-associated virus serotype 9 (scAAV9) vector?
questions.explanation: Onasemnogene abeparvovec is an AAV9-based gene therapy designed to deliver a functional copy of the SMN1 gene to treat spinal muscular atrophy.

questions.q: Voretigene neparvovec is a recombinant adeno-associated virus vector-based gene therapy specifically indicated for the treatment of which inherited condition?
questions.explanation: Voretigene neparvovec delivers a normal copy of the RPE65 gene directly to retinal pigment epithelial cells to treat biallelic RPE65 mutation-associated retinal dystrophy, also known as Leber congenital amaurosis.

questions.q: Which class of viral vector is characterized by its ability to transduce both dividing and non-dividing cells and is derived from a pathogen that causes acquired immunodeficiency syndrome?
questions.explanation: Lentiviruses, a subclass of retroviruses such as HIV-1, possess the unique ability among retroviruses to infect non-dividing cells by actively crossing the intact nuclear membrane.

questions.q: A major characteristic risk or adverse effect associated with the use of early gamma-retroviral vectors integrating into the host genome during ex vivo gene therapy for SCRA-X1 was the development of which condition?
questions.explanation: Early clinical trials using gamma-retroviral vectors for X-linked severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID-X1) resulted in insertional mutagenesis near proto-oncogenes like LMO2, causing clonal T-cell proliferation and leukemia.

questions.q: Which non-viral gene delivery method utilizes a high-voltage electrical pulse to transiently permeabilize the cell membrane, allowing plasmid DNA to enter the cytoplasm?
questions.explanation: Electroporation applies short, high-voltage electrical pulses to create temporary aqueous pores in the lipid bilayer, facilitating the cellular uptake of exogenous DNA or RNA.

questions.q: Talimogene laherparepvec (T-VEC) is a genetically modified oncolytic viral therapy derived from which virus class?
questions.explanation: T-VEC is an oncolytic immunotherapy derived from herpes simplex virus type 1, engineered to selectively replicate within tumors and express GM-CSF to enhance anti-tumor immunity.

games.title: Oncology: Surgery, Radiotherapy & Chemotherapy Explained: drug duel
games.blurb: Drug Duel for Year 3 and above, written fresh today.

questions.q: Which of the following chemotherapeutic agents is an alkylating agent that cross-links DNA and is classically associated with hemorrhagic cystitis?
questions.explanation: Cyclophosphamide is a nitrogen mustard alkylating agent whose metabolite, acrolein, causes urothelial toxicity leading to hemorrhagic cystitis, which is mitigated by mesna.

questions.q: What is the primary dose-limiting toxicity associated with the administration of doxorubicin, an anthracycline chemotherapy drug?
questions.explanation: Doxorubicin generates free radicals that cause cumulative, dose-dependent, and often irreversible cardiomyopathy and heart failure.

questions.q: Which platinum-based antineoplastic agent is most frequently associated with severe nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity, requiring aggressive intravenous hydration?
questions.explanation: Cisplatin causes heavy metal-like cumulative damage to the renal tubules and cochlear hair cells, making nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity its hallmark adverse effects.

questions.q: Which vinca alkaloid is most commonly noted for causing peripheral neuropathy as a major dose-limiting side effect, while typically sparing the bone marrow?
questions.explanation: Vincristine disrupts microtubule assembly in neuronal axons, leading to significant peripheral sensory and motor neuropathy with relatively minimal myelosuppression.

questions.q: Trastuzumab is a monoclonal antibody used primarily in the treatment of breast cancers that overexpress which specific molecular marker?
questions.explanation: Trastuzumab binds to the extracellular domain of the HER2/neu (ERBB2) receptor tyrosine kinase, inhibiting signaling pathways critical for tumor cell proliferation in HER2-positive breast cancer.

questions.q: What is the primary mechanism of action of methotrexate, an antimetabolite frequently used in both oncology and rheumatology?
questions.explanation: Methotrexate competitively inhibits dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR), preventing the reduction of dihydrofolate to tetrahydrofolate and thereby halting purine and thymidine synthesis.

questions.q: Which taxane chemotherapeutic agent stabilizes microtubules against depolymerization and is frequently associated with cumulative fluid retention and hypersensitivity reactions?
questions.explanation: Docetaxel promotes microtubule polymerization and stabilizes them, with characteristic clinical toxicities including severe neutropenia and peripheral fluid retention.

questions.q: Bleomycin is an antitumor antibiotic used in various regimens whose most serious and potentially fatal adverse effect is which of the following?
questions.explanation: Bleomycin causes DNA strand breaks and lacks the enzyme hydrolase in the lungs, making it uniquely prone to inducing cumulative and potentially fatal pulmonary fibrosis.
